passage:
College counselling centre, session note, Wednesday.
Mohit's roommate, Hrithik, walked him to my door this morning and waited outside. Mohit's Dadaji died in Kanpur four months ago. Mohit keeps replaying their last phone call: Dadaji asked when he was coming home, and Mohit said, "After exams, pakka." Dadaji died two weeks before exams ended. Today Mohit said "if only" nine times. If only he had taken the train in October. If only he had skipped the fest. I asked what he could actually have known in October. He said, very quietly, "Nothing. He sounded fine." We talked about how guilt can feel easier than helplessness, because guilt pretends we had control. He cried for the first time in our sessions. Next session is booked for Monday. Hrithik has the centre's number and knows to call if Mohit seems worse before then.

qa.q: How many times did Mohit say "if only" today?
qa.a: Mohit said "if only" nine times.

qa.q: Why might Mohit keep replaying the last phone call?
qa.a: He feels guilty and helpless; blaming himself gives him a sense of control over a death he could not have prevented.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor offer at this stage?
qa.a: The counsellor asks what Mohit could really have known in October, helping him see that the guilt pretends he had control, and books another session.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hrithik to walk Mohit to the centre?
qa.a: Hrithik is probably worried and protective, waiting outside and staying ready to call the centre if Mohit seems worse.

grounding: Shows a young adult looping on the last phone call and what-ifs, with guilt standing in for control over a death that was never in his hands.

passage: It happened in the middle of a statistics lecture, eight months after Ba died. Someone two rows ahead opened a tiffin, and the smell of methi thepla drifted back. Ba made them every Sunday, burnt on one edge because she never trusted the gas. Before I knew it, tears were dripping onto my notebook. I hadn't cried like that since the thirteenth day. I kept my head down and pretended to write. Zainab, sitting next to me, slid a tissue across without looking and whispered, "Hansa, want to step out?" I shook my head. Afterwards I felt ashamed, as if I had gone backwards, as if I had failed some test of being over it. Zainab said her Dadi's death still came back like that, on random Tuesdays, years later. That helped more than anything.

qa.q: What smell drifted back during the lecture?
qa.a: The smell of methi thepla from someone's tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Hansa feel ashamed after the lecture?
qa.a: Hansa felt ashamed and discouraged, as if crying eight months later meant going backwards.

qa.q: What could help Hansa when the next wave comes?
qa.a: Remembering that grief returns in waves, as Zainab described, and that stepping out for a few minutes is allowed.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab, sitting next to Hansa?
qa.a: Zainab recognises the wave from her own loss, so she quietly offers a tissue and a way out without any fuss.

grounding: Shows a smell bringing sudden tears in a lecture months after a death, and the wave feeling like going backwards when it is not.

passage:
Warden's note, girls' hostel, 14 August.
Last week Harsha came to my office with a plan, which surprised me. Today is the first anniversary of her father's death. She said, "I know it'll be a bad day, so I'm not pretending it won't be." She had swapped her mess duty, told her lab partner she would be offline, and arranged to cook his favourite rajma with her roommate in the pantry. This evening I passed the pantry and saw them both at the stove, Harsha crying and stirring at the same time, the roommate passing her chopped onions. Later she stopped by my office and said, "I cried a lot. It's grief, it's allowed. I feel lighter." I told her my door is open tonight and tomorrow too.
Rekha

qa.q: What did Harsha cook with her roommate?
qa.a: Her father's favourite rajma, in the pantry.

qa.q: What does Harsha's remark "It's grief, it's allowed" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels lighter and calmer, accepting the tears as grief rather than weakness.

qa.q: Why did planning the hard date help Harsha?
qa.a: Expecting the bad day, clearing her time and planning a ritual with a friend let the tears come and pass without judgement.

qa.q: What might it be like for the roommate to cook with Harsha while she cries?
qa.a: The roommate stays steady, passing onions, perhaps feeling close and useful rather than awkward.

grounding: Shows a young adult expecting a hard anniversary, planning it with a friend and a ritual, and letting the tears come without judging them.

subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage: The first morning after the funeral, Rosa woke at nine. For two years she had woken at three, then five, listening for her father's cough through the wall of the terraced house in Manchester. Now there was only the rain and a car door somewhere down the street. She lay still and felt something loosen in her chest: relief. A heartbeat later came a hot wave of shame. What kind of daughter feels relieved? She told no one for a week. When Chidi from next door brought soup and asked how she was sleeping, Rosa blurted, "Too well. I hate myself for it." Chidi sat down at the kitchen table. "You loved him, and you were exhausted. My mum said the same after my gran. Both things are true." Rosa cried then, properly, for the first time since the hospital.

qa.q: At what times did Rosa used to wake during the two years of caring?
qa.a: She woke at three, then five, listening for her father's cough.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rosa have that first morning?
qa.a: She felt relief loosening her chest, then a hot wave of shame about feeling relieved at all.

qa.q: What helped Rosa's shame start to lift?
qa.a: Saying it out loud to Chidi, who answered that love and exhaustion can both be true, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Chidi seem to see Rosa's relief?
qa.a: Chidi sees it as normal, not shameful, having heard Chidi's own mum say the same after a gran died.

grounding: Shows a caregiver feeling relief alongside grief after a long illness ends in death, then shame about the relief until it is spoken aloud.

passage:
First year, a Friday. Farhan stood in the kitchen with Abbu's steel ladle and could not lift it. Some days he did not open the shop at all. His sister Noor noticed, and that spring she went with him to a grief counsellor at the community clinic, week after week.
Third year, Eid morning. Farhan made Abbu's biryani, burning the bottom exactly the way Abbu used to. Noor tasted it and laughed, then both of them cried a little over the pot, and then they ate two plates each.
Fourth year, a Sunday. On the terrace Farhan handed his nephew a bowl of grain. "Scatter it wide, like this. These are Abbu's sparrows." The boy asked who Abbu was. Farhan smiled and told him, and the telling did not hurt the way it once had.

qa.q: What did Farhan hand his nephew on the terrace?
qa.a: A bowl of grain to scatter for the sparrows.

qa.q: How had Farhan's feelings about Abbu changed by the fourth year?
qa.a: He could feel warmth alongside the pain, smiling as he told the story, where once he could not even lift the ladle.

qa.q: What turning point helped Farhan move from frozen to carrying on?
qa.a: Seeing a grief counsellor with Noor when the pain had frozen him, and later keeping Abbu's recipe and sparrow habit alive.

qa.q: What might Eid morning have been like for Noor?
qa.a: Noor could laugh and cry over the burnt biryani with her brother, sharing the warmth and the loss together.

grounding: Shows a griever over years moving from frozen pain, with counselling, to keeping a parent's recipe and habit alive with warmth.

passage: "Come, sit with your Pooja Nani while the dal cooks. You asked how to help your friend whose brother died. When I was twenty-five, my dear friend Kamal lost his young wife, Leela. At the funeral, everyone came. Three months later, nobody came. People were afraid to say her name, as if it would break him. So I did a small thing. Every Thursday I went with a tiffin, and I said her name. 'Leela loved this pickle.' 'Leela would laugh at this.' The first time, his eyes filled. By the fifth Thursday he was telling me Leela stories himself. Some weeks we only walked to the lake and back. And I always asked, 'How are you today?' Not in general. Today. It was never one big thing, beta. It was showing up."

qa.q: On which day did Pooja go to Kamal with a tiffin?
qa.a: Every Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep saying Leela's name?
qa.a: She was sad to see Kamal left alone and hoped hearing the name would show him Leela was still remembered.

qa.q: What choice by young Pooja made the difference?
qa.a: Choosing steady small visits, saying Leela's name and asking how he was that day, instead of one big gesture.

qa.q: How did the Thursdays change things for Kamal?
qa.a: Kamal went from tearing up to telling Leela stories himself, likely feeling less alone in his grief.

grounding: Shows a friend who keeps saying the lost person's name, brings meals and walks for months and asks how the mourner is today.

passage:
Monday, June. After class, Ms Elizabeth asked who would lead the debate team this year. Lalremsiami's hand was up before she had finished. "I knew I could count on you," the teacher said, and the words glowed in her chest all the way home through the Aizawl drizzle.
Saturday, two weeks later. Board exam coaching three evenings a week, debate practice on two, and now she had said yes to tutoring the neighbour's twins on Sundays. She coloured her timetable with five highlighters and taped it above her desk. Lights out after one, alarm at five. She felt unstoppable.
Friday, July. Her team won the inter-school debate. In assembly the principal called her "the most reliable student in Class 12". Back home she added two more items to her list and hid a long yawn from her mother.

qa.q: How many highlighters did Lalremsiami use for her timetable?
qa.a: Five highlighters.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when the teacher said "I knew I could count on you"?
qa.a: She felt proud and energised; the praise glowed in her chest all the way home.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: An adult could notice the late nights and praise rest and limits, not only results, and help her drop one commitment.

qa.q: How might Ms Elizabeth see Lalremsiami right now?
qa.a: She likely sees a proud, capable student and may not notice the lost sleep behind the results.

grounding: Shows a high-achieving teen saying yes to exams, coaching, debate and tutoring, cutting sleep while praise keeps her going.

passage: At 11:40 p.m., at her corner desk in the Chennai flat, Charu made her third cold coffee of the day and stirred it with a pencil. Her nose was running again, the fourth cold since term began. On the shelf her veena sat under a dust cover she had not lifted in six weeks. "You used to play every evening," her sister Vidya said from the doorway. "No time," Charu said. "I'm just being lazy. I wasted the whole afternoon staring at one page." She opened the chemistry guide, determined to finish two chapters before sleeping, and read the same paragraph four times. Vidya watched her pinch her own arm to stay awake, then went quietly to wake their mother.

qa.q: How long had Charu's veena stayed under its dust cover?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Charu call herself lazy?
qa.a: She feels frustrated and ashamed of her tiredness, reading exhaustion as laziness, so she pushes harder.

qa.q: What could help Charu at this stage?
qa.a: Seeing the colds, the lost music and the late coffees as signs she needs rest, and talking to a parent or doctor, rather than pushing harder.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to see Charu's late nights?
qa.a: Vidya is worried, remembering Charu playing every evening, and goes to wake their mother.

grounding: Shows a student running on coffee and late nights, catching colds and dropping hobbies, reading the tiredness as laziness and pushing on.

passage:
"You're still colour-coding the survey data?" Lokesh leaned back until his chair creaked. "Gautam, nobody reads final-year projects. The external will flip three pages and sign."
"I just want it to be decent," Gautam said, eyes on the screen.
"Decent." Lokesh laughed without smiling. "Last year I'd have stayed till midnight with you. Now I can't even open the file. What's the point?"
"You built half this model. You loved it in August."
"August me was an idiot. Look at them." He nodded at the next bench, where two classmates were arguing happily over a chart. "Acting like it matters."
Gautam turned from the screen. "You've been saying that about everything lately. The fest, placements, even cricket."
Lokesh rubbed his eyes. "I'm just tired, man. Tired of caring."
"Then maybe that's the thing to talk about. Not the project."

qa.q: What did Lokesh say the external examiner will do?
qa.a: Flip three pages and sign.

qa.q: What feelings might sit underneath Lokesh's sneering at the classmates?
qa.a: He is exhausted and tired of caring; mocking others protects him from caring about work he no longer has the energy for.

qa.q: What could Gautam suggest next?
qa.a: Gautam could gently ask how long Lokesh has felt this tired and suggest talking to a mentor or the college counsellor.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel watching his friend change?
qa.a: He seems concerned and a little hurt, remembering how much Lokesh loved the model in August.

grounding: Shows a final-year student calling the work pointless and sneering at classmates who care, a cynicism that shields an exhausted mind.

passage: The ceiling fan in the electricity board office at Nohar clicked with every turn. Kamal had been on the same meter-reading register since ten. Six months ago he could finish one in forty minutes. Now it was past noon, and he had just found his third wrong entry, a house number copied onto the wrong line. He pressed his palms into his eyes. Fraud, said a voice in his head. They'll find out you were never good at this. He stayed through lunch to redo the page and made a fresh mistake while redoing it. Mehak, at the next desk, slid a glass of chaas towards him. "You've skipped lunch four days running. Is it only the register, or is it everything?" Kamal opened his mouth to say "only the register", and found he couldn't.

qa.q: What mistake had Kamal just found?
qa.a: His third wrong entry, a house number copied onto the wrong line.

qa.q: What does the voice in Kamal's head suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels like a fraud and ashamed, sure others will discover he was never good at the job.

qa.q: Why won't working through lunch fix Kamal's problem?
qa.a: His mistakes come from exhaustion, and harsh self-criticism plus skipped breaks only deepen it; he needs rest and support.

qa.q: What has Mehak noticed about Kamal?
qa.a: Mehak has noticed him skipping lunch four days running and senses the trouble is bigger than one register.

grounding: Shows a worker whose simple tasks now take far longer and whose errors multiply, with self-criticism deepening the exhaustion.
